title: Former NASA executive: current lunar landing plan is too complex, 2028 is fundamentally unrealistic
dek: Doug Cooke argues that the lunar lander relies on unverified cryogenic propellant orbital transfer and a tall, narrow structure, each reducing mission success probability, while China's simplified plan more likely reaches the Moon first.
why: An engineering manager who spent 38 years at NASA and led the Exploration Systems Mission Directorate systematically dissects specific technical flaws in the Artemis lunar architecture rather than vague delays—high information density.
who: Engineers, tech policy observers, and space enthusiasts interested in the US-China lunar race, aerospace engineering management, and major project architecture decisions.
skip: The opening small talk about the guest's personal background, rowing, and collecting interests can be skipped without affecting understanding of the technical arguments.

points.h: Single lunar landing needs ten to twenty-plus launches—simply not credible
points.body: Cooke flatly states that the current Artemis architecture requires ten to twenty-plus rocket launches just to deliver the lunar lander to lunar orbit. ‘That's simply not credible to me.’ He notes that SLS and Orion are already proven, but NASA hasn't used SLS as originally designed. Instead, all complexity has been dumped into the lander and orbital refueling—opposite to the direction he and colleagues studied over thirty years. China's approach, by contrast, aligns more closely with those original research conclusions.

points.h: The lunar lander's cryogenic fuel transfer has never been validated at scale
points.body: Both contractor teams need to transfer large quantities of cryogenic propellant—liquid oxygen, methane, and others—in lunar orbit to give their landers enough thrust to leave orbit and reach the Moon. These fuels evaporate continuously, so the refueling spacecraft must be resupplied repeatedly and quickly before losses mount. Large-scale cryogenic fuel transfer has never been validated before. Cooke says he's been raising this since congressional testimony in 2019; now that landers are selected, the problem is more concrete.

points.h: A lunar lander over 50 meters tall: like standing a pencil on the Moon
points.body: Cooke points out the new lander exceeds 50 meters—an elevator rises roughly 30 yards. Successful past landers—Apollo, prior robotic ones—were squat, low center of gravity, wide footprint: drop a foot into a crater and they stay upright. This tall, narrow design has extremely high center of gravity; lean beyond the footpads and it topples. ‘Like balancing a pencil upright on a table.’ The Moon's south pole is already jagged, shadowed, and its regolith properties remain poorly mapped.

points.h: Returning to Apollo-style storable fuel design would actually work
points.body: Cooke's alternative—Plan B—abandons cryogenic fuel for storable propellants used in Apollo, paired with a shorter, wider lander matching the SLS cargo bay diameter. No reusability required, no new technology invented, just existing techniques. He concedes this approach has lower reuse potential and might not hit 2030, but within that timeframe it would actually be feasible.

points.h: More launches and critical operations means lower overall mission success rate
points.body: Cooke notes each critical operation—orbit insertion, fuel transfer, rendezvous, docking—carries its own success probability. Multiply them together: more operations mean lower overall success. He uses Artemis II as example: even a relatively simple mission demands near-perfect execution on every orbit correction. The current lunar architecture demands far more critical operations than before, further degrading overall mission success.

points.h: Human-scale Mars entry and landing is a technology humanity hasn't solved
points.body: Cooke admits that human-scale Mars Entry, Descent, and Landing (EDL) is a major unproven technology. Mars has a thinner atmosphere than Earth but still needs a heat shield; past robotic landers were much smaller and already pushed systems to their limits. A crewed landing vehicle is vastly larger. ‘This isn't a detail, and it's not a scale we've accomplished before.’

points.h: NASA's engineering talent is hemorrhaging, decisions shift to approve-then-fix
points.body: Cooke says new administrator Jared Isaacman has acknowledged NASA's capabilities have declined. The problem is decision-making has become top-down—decide first, fix later—rather than grounded in solid engineering data. The so-called ‘commercial’ model also denied engineers the deep design participation they had during Space Shuttle and Space Station eras. This drove talented engineers out in last year's buyout wave. ‘They didn't see a path forward, so they left.’

points.h: Artemis III rendezvous without docking is just wasting irreplaceable hardware
points.body: Cooke notes Artemis III plans Orion rendezvous with the lander, but he's heard little about ‘docking.’ Rendezvous itself will be verified in Artemis II with the upper stage. If Artemis III just repeats rendezvous without docking, ‘you're burning through precious hardware.’ The real leap—verifying cryogenic fuel transfer and absorbing the major probability hit—actually falls on the next phase, Artemis IV.

Procurement model where NASA buys completed services from private companies rather than providing deep design oversight.

And when people tell me we're heading straight to Mars, it tells me we're not heading anywhere.
